quick: 25-100 mg PO once daily (HF: start 12.5-25 mg)
Take with or immediately after food
summary: Metoprolol succinate is a once-daily extended-release beta-1 selective blocker used for hypertension, angina pectoris, and chronic heart failure (reduces cardiovascular mortality and HF hospitalizations). It slows heart rate and AV conduction and lowers blood pressure. Therapy must never be stopped abruptly; taper over 1-2 weeks to avoid rebound ischemia.
indications: Hypertension (to lower blood pressure and reduce cardiovascular risk)
Heart failure (to reduce cardiovascular mortality and heart failure hospitalizations)

dosage.d: Initial 25-100 mg daily; max studied 400 mg/day
dosage.n: Titrate at weekly or longer intervals; max effect of a given dose seen after ~1 week

dosage.d: Start 1 mg/kg once daily (max initial 50 mg); doses above 2 mg/kg or 200 mg not studied
dosage.n: Adjust per blood pressure response; not studied under 6 years

dosage.d: Initial 100 mg daily; max studied 400 mg/day
dosage.n: Increase at weekly intervals to optimum response or pronounced HR slowing

dosage.d: Start 25 mg once daily for 2 weeks; titrate up to max 200 mg
dosage.n: Double dose every 2 weeks to highest tolerated; stabilize other HF therapy first

dosage.d: Start 12.5 mg once daily; titrate up to max 200 mg
dosage.n: Monitor closely during up-titration; reduce diuretic if worsening before advancing dose

dosage.d: Use the same total daily dose as extended-release
dosage.n: Conversion of total daily milligram dose

admin: Administer once daily, preferably with or immediately following meals
Scored tablets may be divided but must not be crushed or chewed
Take at approximately the same time each day
Do not interrupt or discontinue without physician advice
When discontinuing, taper the dose gradually over 1-2 weeks
moa: Metoprolol is a beta-1 selective (cardioselective) adrenergic receptor blocker without intrinsic sympathomimetic activity. It slows the sinus rate and decreases AV nodal conduction. Cardioselectivity is relative and diminishes at higher plasma concentrations, where beta-2 receptors (bronchial and vascular) are also inhibited. Antihypertensive effect is attributed to decreased cardiac output, reduced central sympathetic outflow, and suppression of renin activity; antianginal effect is from reduced myocardial oxygen demand.

absolute: Second- or third-degree heart block (greater than first degree)
Sick sinus syndrome without a pacemaker
Known hypersensitivity to any product component
relative: Bronchospastic disease (avoid beta-blockers; use lowest effective dose if unavoidable)
Peripheral vascular disease (may aggravate arterial insufficiency)
Thyrotoxicosis (abrupt withdrawal may precipitate thyroid storm)
monitor: Heart rate and blood pressure during titration
Signs of hypoglycemia in fasting or vomiting patients
Anaphylaxis (patients may be unresponsive to usual epinephrine doses)

preg: Available observational data have not demonstrated a drug-associated risk of major birth defects or miscarriage with metoprolol; however there are inconsistent reports of intrauterine growth restriction, preterm birth, and perinatal mortality with maternal beta-blocker use. Metoprolol crosses the placenta; neonates may be at risk for hypotension, hypoglycemia, bradycardia, and respiratory depression and should be observed. Untreated hypertension/heart failure also carries maternal and fetal risk.
lact: Metoprolol is present in human milk; the estimated relative infant dose is approximately 0.5% to 2% of the mother's weight-adjusted dose. No adverse reactions in breastfed infants have been identified. Monitor the breastfed infant for bradycardia and other signs of beta-blockade.
renal: Systemic availability and half-life in patients with renal failure do not differ to a clinically significant degree from normal subjects. No dosage reduction is needed in chronic renal failure.
hepatic: Metoprolol is eliminated mainly by hepatic biotransformation. In hepatic impairment, consider initiating therapy at low doses and gradually increase dosage to optimize therapy while monitoring closely for adverse events.

major: Strong CYP2D6 inhibitors (quinidine, fluoxetine, paroxetine, propafenone) double metoprolol concentrations and reduce cardioselectivity
Catecholamine-depleting drugs (reserpine, MAO inhibitors) - additive hypotension/bradycardia
Clonidine - beta-blockers may exacerbate rebound hypertension on clonidine withdrawal
moderate: Digitalis glycosides, diltiazem, verapamil - slow AV conduction, increased bradycardia risk
Other antihypertensives - additive blood pressure lowering
minor: Other CYP2D6 inhibitors (moderate/weak) likely to increase metoprolol concentration
interactions.food: Bioavailability is not significantly affected by food; take with or after meals for consistency.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid; alcohol may potentiate hypotension and dizziness.
interactions.diagnostics: May mask tachycardia from hypoglycemia or hyperthyroidism, affecting clinical interpretation.

rare: Worsening angina or myocardial infarction on abrupt withdrawal
emergency: Anaphylaxis unresponsive to usual epinephrine doses

monitoring: Signs and symptoms of worsening heart failure (weight gain, increasing dyspnea)
Blood glucose in diabetic, fasting, or vomiting patients
Clinical status during up-titration and on discontinuation
counsel: Take regularly and continuously as directed, preferably with or immediately after meals
Do not interrupt or stop therapy without consulting your physician
If a dose is missed, take only the next scheduled dose; do not double up
Avoid driving or operating machinery until your response to therapy is known
Contact your physician if you experience difficulty breathing
Inform any physician or dentist that you are taking this medication before surgery
Heart failure patients should report weight gain or worsening shortness of breath
Be aware of hypoglycemia risk if fasting or vomiting
pk: Gradual; antihypertensive effect builds over days
Extended-release: 1/4 to 1/2 of peak from conventional metoprolol
pearls: Never discontinue abruptly; taper over 1-2 weeks to avoid rebound angina/MI, especially in ischemic heart disease
Cardioselectivity is dose-dependent and is lost at higher doses
In heart failure, stabilize other HF therapy and start low (12.5-25 mg) with slow up-titration
Strong CYP2D6 inhibitors double plasma levels - monitor closely
In pheochromocytoma, start an alpha-blocker before the beta-blocker
No dose adjustment needed in renal impairment; hemodialysis does not remove it appreciably
missed: If a dose is missed, take only the next scheduled dose at the usual time. Do not double the dose to make up for a missed one.
overdose: Overdose may cause severe bradycardia, hypotension, cardiogenic shock, AV block, heart failure, bronchospasm, and impaired consciousness. Manage with intensive care: atropine or adrenergic agents/pacemaker for bradycardia, vasopressors (dopamine/norepinephrine) for hypotension, glucagon and adrenergic drugs for heart failure/shock, and bronchodilators for bronchospasm. Hemodialysis is unlikely to be useful.
